issue.title: Links should be able to expire

data.question: Issue #83 doesn't say what makes a Link expire, and the rest of the spec depends on it: what we store, the creation API, how the Redirect responds, and what happens to Short Codes and Clicks. What should trigger expiry? (a) the person shortening the URL picks an optional expiry time for that Link when they create it; (b) one service-wide lifetime applies to every Link (for example, all Links last 30 days); (c) the Link expires after a set number of Clicks; or (d) the Link expires after a period with no Clicks.
data.recommendation: (a) Make it optional and per-Link, set at creation. The shortening request takes an optional expiry as a whole-day lifetime, such as 1 to 365 days, which the service turns into a fixed UTC expiry time. A Link created without one never expires, so every existing Link and client keeps working. Expiry is based only on time, not on Clicks: counting toward a limit would tie the Redirect to the asynchronous Click Recorder, which drops Clicks when it is overloaded, so a Click limit couldn't be enforced exactly. Expiry is checked on every Redirect, which ADR 0005's 302 already makes possible. Follow-up questions will cover the expired-Link response, whether Short Codes can be reused, and what happens to Clicks.

data.question: When someone follows the Short URL of a Link that has expired, how should the Redirect respond? (a) `410 Gone`, a separate answer that says the Link existed but has expired; (b) `404 Not Found`, exactly like an unknown Short Code, so an expired Link can't be told apart from one that never existed; or (c) `302` to a shortener-hosted "this link has expired" page.
data.recommendation:
(a) Use `410 Gone` with a short readable body ("This link has expired") and `Cache-Control: no-store`. HEAD requests get the same response, and no Click is recorded. The 302 path, its Click hand-off and the `404` for unknown Short Codes stay exactly as in specs 0001 and 0003.

Why not (b): ADR 0014's reason for returning `404` was to avoid confirming which Short Codes exist to someone guessing at the stats endpoint. That doesn't apply here, because whoever follows a Short URL was given it. Answering `410` tells them the Link has run out rather than that they mistyped it, which is user story 26's goal of a clear answer.

Why not (c): a `302` to an error page looks like a successful Redirect. It would count as a Click under spec 0003 unless we add a special case, and it hides the failure from API clients and monitoring.

`410` also doesn't depend on the next questions (whether Short Codes can be reused, and what happens to stored Clicks). If expired Links are kept in storage, the answer can stay `410` for as long as they are kept.

data.question: When a Link expires, what happens to it in storage, and can its Short Code ever name a new Link? (a) The expired Link stays stored, its Short Code is retired for good and its Clicks are kept. (b) Expired Links are deleted after a grace period and their Short Codes go back into the pool for new Links. (c) Expired Links are deleted along with their Clicks, but their Short Codes stay retired (we'd keep a list of retired Short Codes).
data.recommendation:
(a) Keep expired Links, never reuse their Short Codes, and keep their Clicks.

Why not (b): reusing a Short Code is risky. People will still have the old Short URL in emails, documents and bookmarks, and once the code is reused it would quietly send them to someone else's Long URL. That's a ready-made phishing path. We also gain almost nothing from it: ADR 0003's 62^7 Short Code space is huge, so Collisions stay rare even if no code is ever freed.

Why not (c): we'd need a new table of retired Short Codes and a background purge job, and we'd throw away Clicks that auditing and R2's per-Link stats (ADR 0014) still need.

What (a) gives us: an expired Short URL answers `410 Gone` for as long as the Link exists, as agreed in the previous answer. Short Code generation and Collision handling stay the same as in spec 0001 and ADR 0003. The Click Recorder and the `clicks` table from spec 0003 are untouched. Expiry needs only one nullable `expires_at` column on `links`, with no job to purge old Links.

Deleting Links and their Clicks, and retaining Clicks for a limited time, stay with R4 and the retention note in spec 0003.
